The Japanese scad, Decapterus maruadsi, is a commercially important carangid species distributed throughout the warm waters of the Indo-West Pacific. In populations from the South China Sea, adults attain a maximum recorded total length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a size that is consistent with values reported for other small-bodied carangids in the region. Growth trajectory analyses based on otolith increment data indicate that this asymptotic length is reached after several years of sustained somatic expansion. The maximum adult wet weight corresponding to this length has been estimated at 270.5 grams [Wwi = 270.5 grams], a value derived from length–weight regressions compiled for the species across its geographic range. This mass places Decapterus maruadsi among the smaller members of its genus, a distinction that may reflect the energetic constraints of its pelagic, schooling lifestyle in subtropical shelf waters. Field surveys have noted that individuals exceeding this mass are exceptionally rare, suggesting that 270.5 grams [Wwi = 270.5 grams] represents a practical physiological ceiling for somatic growth under natural conditions. The species exhibits a moderate growth rate, with juvenile fish showing rapid initial gains that gradually taper as they approach the ultimate length.

Reproductive biology in Decapterus maruadsi is characterized by a relatively early onset of maturation. Puberty, defined here as the attainment of functional gonadal activity, occurs when individuals reach approximately 12.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 12.5 centimeters] in total length. This length is a key life-history threshold, marking the transition from somatic investment toward reproductive capability. Field collections across multiple spawning seasons have consistently shown that individuals below this length are universally immature, while those surpassing it exhibit developing or ripe gonads. The length at puberty represents roughly forty-two percent of the ultimate total length, a proportion that aligns with predictions from life-history theory for moderately productive pelagic species. This early maturation is likely an adaptation to high natural mortality rates experienced by planktivorous schooling fish, favoring an earlier onset of reproduction over extended somatic growth. Juvenile fish thus allocate resources to rapid length increase until the critical size of 12.5 centimeters [Lp = 12.5 centimeters] is achieved, after which energy is increasingly directed toward gamete production.

Fecundity and the chronology of early development are tightly linked to ambient temperature in this species. Spawning occurs during the warmer months, and at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], females produce approximately 291 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 291 eggs per day] over the course of the breeding season. This daily reproductive output, sustained throughout the spawning period, positions Decapterus maruadsi as a highly fecund batch spawner. The interval between successive spawning events under these thermal conditions is brief, with gravid females releasing batches of eggs on nearly a daily basis. The small, buoyant eggs are released into the pelagic environment, where fertilization occurs externally. The maximum daily reproductive rate observed at this temperature underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover, a trait common among small pelagic teleosts that experience fluctuating recruitment success. Continued monitoring of spawning stocks has confirmed that the daily egg production rate remains consistent across consecutive years when thermal regimes are stable.

The earliest life stages of Decapterus maruadsi proceed rapidly under favorable thermal conditions. Yolk-sac larvae begin exogenous feeding at an age of approximately 4.5 days [ab = approximately 4.5 days], when reared at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. The transition to first feeding occurs shortly after yolk-sac resorption, typically within the first week of development. Longevity records for Decapterus maruadsi, derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith age validation, indicate that individuals rarely survive beyond 5 years [am = 5 years] in the wild when water temperatures average 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This maximum lifespan is relatively short compared to many temperate carangids, placing the species firmly among the fast-living, high-mortality end of the life-history continuum. This limited longevity aligns with the species' early maturation and high reproductive output, forming a coherent suite of life-history traits adapted to variable tropical environments. Mortality rates are highest during the larval and early juvenile stages, with the probability of survival increasing markedly after settlement. Older individuals, particularly those approaching five years of age, show signs of reproductive senescence and reduced condition, suggesting that physiological deterioration limits further persistence. The combination of this limited lifespan and high daily fecundity ensures that even modest annual recruitment can sustain population numbers over decadal timescales.
